If you have an off-the-shelf home router, it depends entirely on its feature set and how you go about performing the block. I will list a few things which would all work in the context of a computer acting as a proxy server:

  • The most simple/fundamental thing to do, in the sense that it works at the lowest possible level of the network stack for this task, is to block IP addresses. Almost any good home router should be able to do this because it already has to act upon those addresses in order to perform NAT (look it up) in the first place - you are giving it a list of IP addresses for which it should refuse to forward outbound connections (on a server box, this would be done by adding firewall rules to drop packets if the source or destination is in that list). It would be a research task to determine a full list, and you will very likely have to maintain that list over time.
  • Another approach is to try to thwart domain name resolutions. This is only a soft block for a couple of reasons (client PCs can be configured not to use the router for DNS + doesn't actually stop connections going out to the service via raw IP), but your setup may be simple enough that this works. This is basically like editing your 'hosts' file (/etc/hosts on Linux, some other place on Windows), but doing it at the router.
  • A much more intrusive approach would be some sort of active packet analysis which prevents forwarding if it matches some profile for initiating a connection to that particular service. This doesn't work at all if the payload is already encrypted (such as with TLS as many connections are), and even if not it is still a very bad idea because it will lag every connection to any service - same reason that online gaming is unplayable with particular anti-virus packages active.
